title: UniHam: A Large-Scale SOC-Complete Dataset and Benchmark for Hamiltonian Learning in Materials
authors: Yuewen Huang, Pin Chen, Yutong Lu
abstract: Accurate prediction of electronic Hamiltonians would enable broad property inference while avoiding the high computational cost of Density Functional Theory (DFT). However, progress toward general-purpose materials foundation models is limited by a data bottleneck: existing Hamiltonian datasets are typically small, lack structural diversity, and often omit essential relativistic physics such as spin--orbit coupling (SOC). We therefore construct UniHam, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset and benchmark suite comprising 100,000+ DFT-computed complex-valued Hermitian Hamiltonians with full SOC, covering 72 elements and a wide range of crystal geometries and symmetries (spanning diverse lattice types and space-group families). Building on UniHam, we benchmark two representative state-of-the-art models under a standardized protocol and introduce complementary evaluation metrics that jointly assess three dimensions: (i) Hamiltonian reconstruction accuracy, (ii) out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization across composition/symmetry shifts, and (iii) the ability to support downstream property prediction from the predicted Hamiltonians. Experiments on UniHam demonstrate that the proposed benchmark and metrics effectively differentiate model capabilities, revealing intrinsic SOC- and element-dependent failure modes, large variations in compositional OOD robustness, and the necessity of spectral-level evaluation to assess whether Hamiltonian predictions reliably support downstream electronic-structure properties. Overall, UniHam provides a reproducible, SOC-complete benchmark that can sharpen model comparisons and accelerate the development of next-generation foundation models for quantum materials.

infographic.key_insight: UniHam benchmarks Hamiltonian learning with full spin–orbit coupling (SOC), revealing why reconstruction accuracy alone cannot establish reliability for electronic-property prediction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable learned Hamiltonians could reduce reliance on costly DFT calculations while supporting electronic-property inference across diverse materials.
method: Construct 100,000+ DFT-computed complex-valued Hermitian Hamiltonians with full SOC across 72 elements.
Benchmark two representative state-of-the-art models under a standardized protocol.
Evaluate reconstruction, composition/symmetry out-of-distribution generalization, and downstream property prediction.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations reveal SOC- and element-dependent failure modes, substantial differences in compositional OOD robustness, and the need for spectral-level assessment.
infographic.watch_item: Broad dataset coverage does not guarantee transfer to unseen materials; validate spectral and downstream-property accuracy under relevant distribution shifts.
infographic.paper_title: UniHam: A Large-Scale SOC-Complete Dataset and Benchmark for Hamiltonian Learning in Materials

title: Strain-dependent Dynamics of Interactions of Iodine-vacancy pairs in CsPbI3: A DFT and Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics Study
authors: Donggeun Kang, Seongju Lee, Yonggoon Jeon
abstract: Iodine-vacancy migration and association are important factors in the structural stability of halide perovskites. Although neighboring vacancies have been suggested to form energetically favorable pairs, their stability and reconfiguration under finite-temperature lattice deformation remain unclear. Here, we combine machine-learning molecular dynamics (MLMD) and density functional theory (DFT) to investigate neighboring iodine vacancies in tilted CsPbI3 under isotropic and biaxial strain. The MLMD trajectories reveal a nonmonotonic dependence of short-time hopping fractions on strain, with strong isotropic compression favoring point-like separation and tension promoting pair-preserving relay hopping. Notably, biaxial compression produces distinct orientation-dependent responses: vacancy pairs initially aligned with the compressed plane preferentially undergo separation, whereas those perpendicular to the plane predominantly exhibit relay hopping. Complementary static calculations using DFT and the SevenNet-0 potential yield repulsive interactions for all configurations examined. These findings highlight the importance of finite-temperature dynamics and strain-dependent local geometry in understanding vacancy-pair stability and reconfiguration in halide perovskites.

infographic.key_insight: Strain controls how neighboring iodine vacancies reconfigure in CsPbI3, with compression favoring separation and tension favoring pair-preserving relay hopping under isotropic deformation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Strain and vacancy-pair orientation may offer design levers for managing defect migration and structural stability in halide perovskites.
method: Machine-learning molecular dynamics of neighboring iodine vacancies in tilted CsPbI3.
Isotropic and biaxial strain to probe hopping and pair reconfiguration.
Static DFT and SevenNet-0 calculations of vacancy interactions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trajectories show nonmonotonic short-time hopping fractions and orientation-dependent responses to biaxial compression, while static calculations find repulsive interactions in every configuration examined.
infographic.watch_item: Short-time hopping behavior does not establish long-term vacancy-pair stability or device-scale degradation rates.
infographic.paper_title: Strain-dependent Dynamics of Interactions of Iodine-vacancy pairs in CsPbI3: A DFT and Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics Study

title: Benchmarking language models and agents for scientific reasoning in evolving materials laboratories
authors: Xuyu Dong, Yixuan Li, Jianguo Huang, Feng Chen, Yiyun Zhou, Bo An
abstract: Large language models and the multi-agent systems built around them could accelerate materials discovery by connecting scientific knowledge with experimental decisions. Existing benchmarks establish capabilities in domain knowledge, multimodal interpretation and scientific tool use. As language models increasingly support materials research workflows, their ability to distinguish closely related material states and reason accurately with quantitative evidence remains insufficiently evaluated. These abilities are essential for comparing material responses, assessing mechanisms and maintaining reliable judgements as experimental evidence accumulates. We introduce MatScope to evaluate three connected capabilities. M1 tests unaided, condition-specific reasoning through 200 tasks spanning ten research functions, using aluminium and high-entropy alloys as representative material systems. M2 tests agent-assisted transfer of related knowledge to unresolved materials questions. MatEvoBench-20 tests initial forecasts across scientific dependency chains and revisions of still-hidden responses as observations accumulate. Across eleven model deployments, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, given-input calculations and many physical explanations are handled well. Fine-grained response estimates, comparisons between similar states and quantitatively supported choices remain substantially weaker. Related literature improves selected estimates, while condition and baseline mismatches limit transfer. Progressive observations calibrate some downstream responses and destabilize earlier accurate predictions. MatScope establishes measurable targets for developing reliable scientific reasoning in future self-evolving materials laboratories and materials-aware world models.

infographic.key_insight: Language models handle many materials calculations and physical explanations well but struggle with fine-grained state comparisons and quantitatively justified decisions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable AI-assisted materials discovery requires condition-aware reasoning and evidence updates that improve predictions without destabilizing previously accurate ones.

M2 evaluates agent-assisted transfer of related knowledge to unresolved materials questions.

infographic.paper_title: Benchmarking language models and agents for scientific reasoning in evolving materials laboratories

title: MOTIF: LLM-Defined Material Taxonomies for OOD Property Prediction via Invariant Feature Selection
authors: Gwangseon Jang, Sieun Yun, Dong Ho Lee, Kyong-Ha Lee, Chanuk Lim, Jin Woo Choi
abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization remains a central challenge in materials property prediction, where models must extrapolate to novel chemistries beyond the training distribution. While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong scientific reasoning, their direct use for quantitative prediction remains limited. To address this, we systematically evaluate multiple roles for LLM assistance, finding that only taxonomy-based grouping consistently improves OOD generalization over a strong kNN+GBT baseline. Building on this, we here propose MOTIF, a framework that leverages LLMs not as predictors, but as generators of candidate taxonomies that partition materials into chemically meaningful environments. These taxonomies are evaluated via training-only pseudo-OOD validation, and only those that improve generalization are retained. Invariant feature selection is then applied within each accepted taxonomy, followed by gated aggregation across taxonomies. We evaluate on 2D halide perovskites, where bandgap prediction must generalize across distinct organic spacer families. On this benchmark, MOTIF reduces mean OOD MAE from 0.122 to 0.111 eV. Under a frozen dev/test protocol, the deployable configuration further improves errors from 0.123 to 0.117 eV (electronic bandgap) and from 0.181 to 0.173 eV (optical bandgap). Beyond this primary task, we validate transferability across additional materials datasets, including 3D perovskite solar cell efficiencies and Matbench benchmarks with structure-based splits. Across domains, MOTIF consistently improves robustness under distribution shift, outperforming expert-defined groupings, rule-based heuristics, and clustering baselines, while remaining competitive with strong classical selection methods. These results demonstrate that LLMs are most effective not as predictors, but as tools for discovering structure in data.

infographic.key_insight: MOTIF improves out-of-distribution materials property prediction by using LLM-generated taxonomies to guide invariant feature selection, rather than using LLMs as numerical predictors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can improve prediction robustness for unfamiliar material chemistries, supporting screening beyond the training distribution.
method: Generate candidate chemically meaningful material taxonomies with LLMs.
Retain taxonomies that improve training-only pseudo-OOD validation.
Apply invariant feature selection within each accepted taxonomy and combine predictions through gated aggregation.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 2D halide perovskites, mean OOD bandgap MAE fell from 0.122 to 0.111 eV; frozen dev/test evaluation also showed smaller improvements for electronic and optical bandgaps, with transfer evaluated on additional materials datasets.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment requires leakage-free taxonomy selection and validation that pseudo-OOD gains transfer to the intended chemistry shift.
infographic.paper_title: MOTIF: LLM-Defined Material Taxonomies for OOD Property Prediction via Invariant Feature Selection

title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
authors: Klemens Flöge, Simon Bing, Leo Grinsztajn, Eliott Kalfon, Lennart Purucker, Noah Hollmann
abstract: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: Tabular foundation models can serve as highly competitive, out-of-the-box surrogates for Bayesian optimization in materials discovery.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These models could simplify materials-search workflows by reducing reliance on task-specific Gaussian process kernels and hyperparameter tuning.
method: Use TabPFN and TabICL as Bayesian optimization surrogate models.
Evaluate on two standard materials science benchmarks.
Compare against Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports highly competitive performance across two benchmarks without task-specific active-learning training or GP kernel selection.
infographic.watch_item: Results from two benchmarks do not establish reliability across broader materials domains or real laboratory campaigns.
infographic.paper_title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery

title: Effect of Correlation on the Pressure-Induced Insulator to Metal Transition in Complex Spin-Orbit Coupled Double Perovskite La$_2$CoIr$_{1-x}$Ti$_x$O$_6$
authors: Vineeta Yadav, Sromona Nandi, Rudra Sekhar Manna
abstract: We study the effect of electron correlation ($U$) and hydrostatic pressure on the electronic properties of double perovskites La$_2$CoIr$_{1-x}$Ti$_x$O$_6$ for $x$ = 0, 0.5, and 1, using first-principles electronic structure calculations within density functional theory (DFT). At ambient pressure, we systematically vary the electron correlation, i.e., on-site Coulomb interaction to study its effect on band gap and structural parameters. Increasing the value of $U$ enhances the band gap of all three compositions while producing only a slight variation in structural parameters. The effect of hydrostatic pressure is also studied for the same compositions. The estimated band gap values at ambient pressure closes at approximately 39, 42, and 53 GPa for $x$ = 0 (for $U_\mathrm{Co}$ = 5 eV and $U_\mathrm{Ir}$ = 2 eV), 0.5 (for $U_\mathrm{Co}$ = 5 eV and $U_\mathrm{Ir}$ = 2 eV), and 1 (for $U_\mathrm{Co}$ = 4 eV), respectively, indicating pressure-induced insulator-to-metal transitions. These results show that electron correlation stabilises the insulating state, whereas hydrostatic pressure favours the metallic state by closing the band gap. These findings highlight the tunability of correlated oxides through electron correlations and pressure, offering insights for materials design.

infographic.key_insight: Electron correlation strengthens the insulating state in La₂CoIr₁₋ₓTiₓO₆, while hydrostatic pressure closes the band gap and drives a predicted insulator-to-metal transition.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Composition and pressure offer routes to tune electronic behavior in correlated double perovskites for materials design.
method: First-principles density functional theory calculations for x = 0, 0.5, and 1.
Varied on-site Coulomb interaction U to assess band gaps and structural parameters at ambient pressure.
Applied hydrostatic pressure to predict band-gap closure.
infographic.evidence_signal: Calculated gaps close near 39, 42, and 53 GPa for x = 0, 0.5, and 1, respectively, using UCo = 5 eV and UIr = 2 eV for the first two compositions and UCo = 4 eV for x = 1.
infographic.watch_item: Transition pressures are computational predictions at specified U values; experimental validation is not reported in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Effect of Correlation on the Pressure-Induced Insulator to Metal Transition in Complex Spin-Orbit Coupled Double Perovskite La$_2$CoIr$_{1-x}$Ti$_x$O$_6$

title: Quantum Embedding from Molecular to Crystalline Environments at the Cost of a Gas-Phase Calculation
authors: Manas Sharma, Marek Sierka
abstract: We present a direct-space formulation and implementation of quantum density functional theory (DFT) embedding for molecular active subsystems embedded in frozen environments (hosts) of arbitrary dimensionality, from finite molecular hosts to extended systems. The host is computed once without the embedded molecule (the guest) and is represented only by its electron density fitted in an atom-centered auxiliary Gaussian basis together with its nuclear charges with the periodic electrostatics separated into an explicit near-field and a continuous fast-multipole far-field operator. The method allows the removal of host atoms from this representation to create vacancies or other voids without requiring a supercell creation. Analytic nuclear gradients are also implemented, enabling structural relaxation of the active subsystem. We demonstrate the versatility of the approach through applications to adsorbates on periodic surfaces and molecules embedded in bulk solvent environments. For CO on MgO(001), we show that DFT-in-DFT converges rapidly and reproduces the periodic interaction energy within 0.44 kJ/mol while reducing the cost by a factor of 27. Real-time time-dependent embedded DFT (RT-TDDFET) of methylenecyclopropene in periodic water is showcased to produce a ~0.6 eV solvatochromic blue shift, while strong-field propagation of CO2 on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) yields substrate-induced effects at the cost of a gas-phase propagation. Coupling the embedding scheme to excited-state correlated wave function theory methods such as CC2 yields a solvent shift within 0.01 eV of supermolecular CC2 references, while reducing the computational cost by over 500 times.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum embedding captures molecular behavior in environments ranging from finite hosts to periodic crystals while keeping active-subsystem calculations near gas-phase cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables lower-cost simulations of adsorption, solvation, structural relaxation, and light-driven molecular dynamics in materials environments.
method: Compute the host once and freeze its electron density in an atom-centered auxiliary Gaussian representation.
Treat periodic electrostatics with explicit near-field and fast-multipole far-field operators, allowing host atoms to be removed without constructing supercells.
Use analytic nuclear gradients for relaxation and couple embedding to real-time TDDFT or correlated excited-state methods such as CC2.
infographic.evidence_signal: For CO/MgO(001), embedding reproduced the periodic interaction energy within 0.44 kJ/mol at 27× lower cost; embedded CC2 solvent shifts agreed within 0.01 eV of supermolecular references at over 500× lower cost.
infographic.watch_item: The frozen-host approximation does not self-consistently update the environment in response to the guest, so strongly responsive hosts require careful validation.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Embedding from Molecular to Crystalline Environments at the Cost of a Gas-Phase Calculation

title: Defects and Structural Evolution in CrSBr: Machine-Learning Potentials for Atomistic Simulations
authors: Arsalan Hashemi, Daniil Kruklinskii, Xiaoya Chang, Tapio Ala-Nissila, Mikko Karttunen, Arkady V. Krasheninnikov
abstract: The layered van der Waals semiconductor CrSBr combines intrinsic magnetic order with semiconducting and optical properties, making it a promising material for multifunctional electronic and photonic applications. Understanding how defects and structural transformations affect its properties under experimentally relevant conditions, however, remains challenging for first-principles simulations due to the relevant length and time scales. Here, we develop and benchmark machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) for the Cr-S-Br system, enabling large-scale atomistic simulations of CrSBr with accuracy approaching that of density functional theory (DFT). The charge-aware variant qNEP achieves near-DFT accuracy in predicting lattice constants, formation enthalpies, vacancy energetics, and the anisotropic pressure response of o-CrSBr. Nudged elastic band calculations reveal that pre-existing S vacancies lower the Cr Frenkel-pair migration barrier by up to 1.1 eV, providing an atomistic mechanism for beam-induced Cr redistribution and structural transformations. Displacement threshold calculations further show that Br is the most susceptible species to electron-beam-induced displacement, identifying the relative ease of removing different atomic species. Together, these results establish a validated computational framework for investigating atomic-scale disorder and structural transformations in CrSBr, providing a basis for defect engineering in materials for future magneto-optoelectronic applications.

infographic.key_insight: Charge-aware machine-learning potentials enable near-DFT-accuracy CrSBr simulations, revealing that sulfur vacancies can lower chromium Frenkel-pair migration barriers by up to 1.1 eV.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports defect engineering and analysis of electron-beam-driven structural changes in CrSBr for potential magneto-optoelectronic devices.
method: Develop and benchmark Cr–S–Br machine-learning interatomic potentials, including charge-aware qNEP.
Use nudged elastic band calculations to evaluate defect migration barriers.
Calculate atomic displacement thresholds to compare species susceptibility to electron-beam damage.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports near-DFT accuracy for qNEP across lattice constants, formation enthalpies, vacancy energetics, and anisotropic pressure response, and identifies Br as the easiest species to displace.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy for structures and conditions outside the benchmarked domain requires further validation before predictive use.
infographic.paper_title: Defects and Structural Evolution in CrSBr: Machine-Learning Potentials for Atomistic Simulations

title: High Pressure Material Phase Identification with Gaussian Kernel Neural Networks
authors: Cameron Ryan, Yasantha Pasindu Hetti Kankanamalage, Shuai Zhang
abstract: Phase identification is a computational task involving the classification of material structure using the positions of atoms. Using data from Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations, our task is to identify the material phase of a set of atoms, based on how the simulations predict their positioning relative to each other. By leveraging existing research on mechanistic neural network theory, particularly Neural Tangent Kernels (NTK), we develop a new and efficient method for classifying simulated material samples. Our method involves defining a set of "atom detectors" that are given positions around the origin in cartesian coordinates. The sum of Gaussians centered at each atom is calculated at each atom detector, and is used as the input to a neural network. We present theoretical and experimental evidence to show that this method is highly effective and efficient at the task. Our method obtains better or similar accuracy scores to commonly used methods while having a major computational speedup.

infographic.key_insight: Gaussian atom-density features enable neural networks to identify material phases with comparable or better accuracy and a major computational speedup over commonly used methods.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster phase identification could reduce the computational cost of analyzing high-pressure molecular dynamics simulations.
method: Place atom detectors at Cartesian positions around the origin.
At each detector, evaluate a sum of Gaussians centered on the atoms.
Feed these features into a neural network, guided by Neural Tangent Kernel theory.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical support and experiments on molecular dynamics data, but provides no numerical accuracy or speedup results.
infographic.watch_item: Robustness across materials and sensitivity to detector placement and Gaussian width require verification.
infographic.paper_title: High Pressure Material Phase Identification with Gaussian Kernel Neural Networks

title: Learning Electronic Band Structures Across the s, p, d Blocks with an Empirical Pseudopotential Network
authors: Qiang Zhu
abstract: Electronic band structures govern how crystals conduct electrons and absorb light. Density-functional theory (DFT) computes them through costly self-consistent iterations, while existing machine-learning models either predict isolated scalar properties or output Hamiltonians that still require DFT solvers. Here we present EpNet, a learned empirical pseudopotential for crystals spanning 63 elements across the \textit{s}, \textit{p} and \textit{d} blocks. An equivariant neural network builds its Hamiltonian from physics-motivated local potentials and nonlocal projectors. Trained solely on band energies, EpNet predicts complete band structures directly from atomic coordinates. On unseen chemical systems, its median errors are \winAll\ eV for band energies and \gapAll\ eV for band gaps. On 600,000 structures from an independent database, its band-gap errors are overall less than half those of existing models, at about 1\% of DFT cost. EpNet thus enables fast screening of electronic properties for materials discovery and electronic-structure simulations of large systems.

infographic.key_insight: EpNet predicts complete crystal band structures directly from atomic coordinates using a learned empirical pseudopotential spanning 63 elements across the s, p and d blocks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fast band-structure and band-gap predictions could accelerate electronic-materials screening at about 1% of DFT computational cost.
method: Use an equivariant neural network to construct a Hamiltonian from local potentials and nonlocal projectors.
Train solely on band energies rather than DFT-derived Hamiltonian labels.
Predict band structures without costly DFT self-consistent iterations.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 600,000 structures from an independent database, the abstract reports overall band-gap errors less than half those of existing models.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract leaves median band-energy and band-gap errors as unresolved placeholders, limiting assessment of absolute accuracy on unseen chemical systems.
infographic.paper_title: Learning Electronic Band Structures Across the s, p, d Blocks with an Empirical Pseudopotential Network

title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction
authors: Makoto Takamoto, Chaitanya Sampara, Viktor Zaverkin, Daniel Oñoro-Rubio, Mathias Niepert
abstract: It is well established that molecular substructures can contribute unequally to chemical and physical properties, with specific motifs or side chains often playing dominant roles. Fragment-based representations have therefore emerged as an effective strategy for incorporating chemically meaningful inductive biases, as exemplified by molecular fingerprints and fragment-based attention mechanisms. However, many existing fragmentation-based machine learning methods rely on predefined chemical rules, which may yield suboptimal fragmentation for previously unseen or chemically unfamiliar structures and often overlook the importance of multiscale molecular representations. To address these limitations, we formulate molecular fragmentation as a radius-constrained optimization problem inspired by the k-center formulation, where the number of clusters is not fixed a priori but emerges from the specified radius, and propose a geometry-based fragmentation method that partitions arbitrary molecular or material structures using largely geometric information, without relying on predefined chemical fragmentation rules. The method provides flexible control over fragment size, enabling the construction of multiscale fragment representations for scale-adaptive modeling. Building on this framework, we develop a geometric fragment-based attention mechanism that integrates multiscale structural information and incorporate it into a multimodal machine learning model combining p-SMILES representations with three-dimensional (3D) conformational information. Experiments on a benchmark polymer dataset show that incorporating 3D conformational information improves prediction accuracy for several properties over models based exclusively on p-SMILES representations. Explainable artificial intelligence analyses further provide insights into the physical relevance of the learned representations.

infographic.key_insight: Geometry-based fragmentation creates adjustable, multiscale molecular representations without predefined chemical fragmentation rules for polymer property prediction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining polymer sequence representations with 3D fragment information can improve prediction of properties influenced by molecular structure at different scales.
method: Partition structures using a radius-constrained optimization inspired by k-center clustering.
Vary the radius to control fragment size and construct multiscale representations.
Integrate geometric fragment attention with p-SMILES and 3D conformational information.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a benchmark polymer dataset, adding 3D conformational information improved accuracy for several properties over p-SMILES-only models; explainability analyses explored the physical relevance of learned representations.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify accuracy gains or establish robustness to conformer selection and unfamiliar polymer chemistries.
infographic.paper_title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction

title: Inverse design of superconductors and semiconductors with differentiable foundation models
authors: Cristóbal Méndez, Justin Tahmassebpur, Tomás A. Arias
abstract: Designing a crystal for a target property requires choosing its elements, stoichiometry, and atomic structure together, yet gradients exist only for the continuous structural variables. We introduce differentiable Equiformer fast effective-atom theory (DEFEAT), which lets a pretrained EquiformerV3 foundation model accept continuous species weights and site occupancies without retraining on fractional data, thereby enabling gradient-based materials optimization. Gradients from fine-tuned property models and a machine-learned energy penalty then guide updates to composition, atom count, atomic positions, and lattice vectors in a single optimization. In a search for phonon-mediated superconductors, density-functional perturbation theory on 45 structurally novel designs gives isotropic Allen-Dynes critical temperatures above 10 K for 39; the highest is 24.0 K for ZrTiNb2CN3, and H4LiPd3 (23.2 K) lies on the static DFT hull. In searches for photovoltaic absorbers, SCAN calculations confirm ten novel crystal structures with band gaps within 20% of a 1.34 eV target on their respective raw or empirically corrected scales, all within 70 meV/atom of the DFT hull, and show that the systematic gap error of the training functional propagates into the designs unless the objective corrects for it. Quasiharmonic free energies from machine-learned potentials further show that finite-temperature competition with solid phases can reorder candidates relative to the static hull.

infographic.key_insight: DEFEAT enables gradient-based inverse crystal design by jointly optimizing composition, atom count, atomic positions, and lattice vectors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports targeted searches for superconductors and photovoltaic absorbers while incorporating an energy penalty to discourage unfavorable structures.
method: Extend a pretrained EquiformerV3 model to continuous species weights and site occupancies without retraining on fractional data.
Combine gradients from fine-tuned property models with a machine-learned energy penalty.
Validate candidates using first-principles calculations and assess finite-temperature phase competition.
infographic.evidence_signal: DFPT yielded isotropic Allen–Dynes critical temperatures above 10 K for 39 of 45 structurally novel designs; SCAN confirmed ten novel absorber structures within 20% of a 1.34 eV target on raw or corrected gap scales, all within 70 meV/atom of the DFT hull.
infographic.watch_item: Training-functional band-gap bias can propagate into designs unless corrected in the objective, and finite-temperature phase competition can change static-hull rankings.
infographic.paper_title: Inverse design of superconductors and semiconductors with differentiable foundation models

title: Sage-Taiyi: A Metacognitive Architecture for Scientific Discovery
authors: Weida Wang, Benteng Chen, Yigeng Jiang, Shuchen Pu, Weiping Shen, Zichao Liu
abstract: We introduce Sage-Taiyi, a metacognition-inspired architecture that uses accumulated scientific understanding to guide what to investigate next and how to investigate it. Through explicit monitoring and control, the system revises its understanding of evidence, assumptions, and unresolved questions, then uses these assessments to adapt research targets and select reusable reasoning methods. On Taiyi-Bench, an AI co-scientist ideation benchmark comprising 265 tasks from 50 papers across ten disciplines, Sage-Taiyi ranks first on all eight metrics of historical rediscovery and open-ended ideation, achieving an Overall score of 54.0 compared with 47.9 for the strongest baseline, AI Scientist-v2. It also performs well on two external scientific ideation benchmarks. Five expert-guided collaborations further connect its proposals to experimental and computational validation across chemistry, materials science, and engineering. In chemistry, reaction-condition optimization raises the yield of cobalt-catalyzed carbonylation from trace amounts to 84% and photocatalytic allylic amination from 13% to 69%. These results support metacognitive regulation as an approach to scientific ideation and its progression toward practical validation.

infographic.key_insight: Sage-Taiyi uses metacognitive monitoring and control to adapt scientific research targets and reasoning methods as its understanding evolves.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture could guide materials and engineering investigations by connecting scientific ideation with expert-led experimental and computational validation.
method: Track evidence, assumptions, and unresolved scientific questions.
Use these assessments to revise research targets and select reusable reasoning methods.
Advance selected proposals through expert-guided validation.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Taiyi-Bench’s 265 tasks from 50 papers across ten disciplines, Sage-Taiyi ranked first on all eight metrics, scoring 54.0 Overall versus 47.9 for AI Scientist-v2; five expert-guided collaborations provided practical validation.
infographic.watch_item: Five expert-guided collaborations do not establish broad autonomous reliability or generalizable gains in materials discovery.
infographic.paper_title: Sage-Taiyi: A Metacognitive Architecture for Scientific Discovery

title: Strain Controlled Hydrogen Interstitial Site Preference and Hydride Phase Suppression in Epitaxial Vanadium
authors: Xin Xiao
abstract: Understanding hydrogen behavior in transition metals is crucial for energy storage and sensing technologies. Here we combine density functional theory (DFT) calculations with in-situ electrical measurements to reveal how epitaxial strain governs hydrogen interstitial site selection and phase stability in vanadium. Our calculations demonstrate a robust thermodynamic preference for tetrahedral (T) over octahedral (O) sites, with the energy difference modulated by lattice anisotropy through strain-tunable H 1s-V 3d orbital hybridization. Experimentally, epitaxial V films on MgO(001) exhibit a critical thickness-dependent crossover: 50 nm films show characteristic first-order alpha-beta hydride transitions, while 10 nm films display continuous solid-solution behavior with complete transition suppression. This crossover is governed by the progressive relaxation of epitaxial strain with increasing film thickness: the 10 nm films retain strong coherent strain that flattens the free-energy landscape and suppresses hydride nucleation, whereas the 50 nm films approach the strain-relaxed bulk limit where long-range elastic interactions restore first-order phase behavior. Finite-size truncation of elastic fields and interfacial electronic reconstruction further reinforce this dimensional crossover. Our work establishes a unified framework connecting atomic-scale orbital physics to mesoscopic phase thermodynamics, providing design principles for strain-engineered metal-hydride systems.

infographic.key_insight: Epitaxial strain tunes hydrogen’s preference for tetrahedral over octahedral sites in vanadium and suppresses the first-order hydride transition in strongly strained thin films.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Film thickness and epitaxial strain offer design levers for controlling hydrogen uptake and phase stability in metal-hydride storage and sensing devices.
method: DFT calculations of hydrogen interstitial energetics and H 1s–V 3d hybridization.
In-situ electrical measurements of epitaxial vanadium films on MgO(001).
Comparison of 10 nm and 50 nm films to probe thickness-dependent phase behavior.
infographic.evidence_signal: Calculations favor tetrahedral hydrogen sites, while electrical measurements show first-order alpha–beta transitions in 50 nm films but continuous solid-solution behavior in 10 nm films.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify strain or independently separate its effects from finite-size and interfacial contributions.
infographic.paper_title: Strain Controlled Hydrogen Interstitial Site Preference and Hydride Phase Suppression in Epitaxial Vanadium

title: DFT-Agent Bench: Scaffold Effects and Execution Provenance in Autonomous DFT
authors: Shijie Liu, Jin Yang, Weilin Wan, Jingtao Han, Jia LI, Tianqi Deng
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for first-principles materials simulation. We report empirical findings from DFT-Agent Bench, a benchmark of 200+ Quantum ESPRESSO tasks spanning relaxation, electronic structure, equation-of-state, and elastic-tensor pipelines over multiple material tiers. Each task carries a QE-derived ground truth with public-reference cross-checks where available, and a provenance audit checks whether the required QE execution contract was met. Under one execution harness, we compare a near-bare ReAct baseline with a bundled v5.1 scaffold on two models. The complete scaffold improves bands+DOS by +0.08/+0.11 and d-electron vc-relax by +0.17 on both models, while high-scoring relaxation and equation-of-state cells leave little room for improvement. The elastic result is model-dependent (0.18 to 0.40 for deepseek-v4-pro and 0.62 to 0.59 for claude-opus-4-8). A fixed 100-task analysis with retrieval disabled supports the aggregate pattern: the fully frozen DeepSeek comparison gains +0.17, while the Opus comparison gains +0.10 against a historical pool baseline (p < 0.001). The provenance gate catches incomplete or unmarked executions that can receive high rubric scores; it is an execution-contract check, not a test for intentional fraud. These results characterize the evaluated DFT workflows. The anonymous review artifact contains the frozen diagnostic slice, prompts, scorer, and solver revisions: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/231e31re91287h/README.md.

infographic.key_insight: A bundled agent scaffold improves autonomous DFT performance on selected workflows, but gains depend on the task and model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable AI-driven materials simulation needs both workflow scaffolding and execution-provenance checks, since high rubric scores can mask incomplete calculations.
method: Benchmark 200+ Quantum ESPRESSO tasks across relaxation, electronic structure, equation-of-state, and elastic-tensor workflows.
Compare near-bare ReAct and bundled v5.1 scaffolds on two models under one execution harness.
Evaluate against QE-derived ground truth and audit compliance with the required execution contract.
infographic.evidence_signal: A fixed 100-task, retrieval-disabled analysis found gains of +0.17 for a fully frozen DeepSeek comparison and +0.10 for Opus against a historical pool baseline (p < 0.001).
infographic.watch_item: Benefits are not uniform: elastic-workflow scores rose from 0.18 to 0.40 for DeepSeek but fell from 0.62 to 0.59 for Opus; provenance checks assess execution compliance, not intent.
infographic.paper_title: DFT-Agent Bench: Scaffold Effects and Execution Provenance in Autonomous DFT

title: X-ray parametric down-conversion probes radiation-induced dynamics in hybrid perovskite MAPbBr3
authors: S. Sofer, O. Sefi, G. J. Man, H. N. Barad, N. P. Jasti, D. Cahen
abstract: We report minute-timescale time-resolved measurements of X-ray parametric down-conversion (PDC) of X-rays into ultraviolet photons in a MAPbBr3 single crystal under continuous irradiation. Despite the known radiation sensitivity of hybrid perovskites and the high photon flux required to detect the intrinsically weak PDC signal, the nonlinear response remains measurable throughout the irradiation sequence. Both PDC and Bragg diffraction exhibit a slow decay consistent with diffusion-driven damage dynamics on timescales reported for bromide-vacancy and proton migration. However, despite their similar decay rates, the PDC and Bragg signals evolve toward markedly different steady states, while an additional fast decay component is observed in the Bragg response but absent in the PDC signal. Density functional theory calculations identify N 2s states of the methylammonium cation as the most likely contributors to the measured PDC response and show that their Fourier component is only weakly affected by bromide-vacancy formation. These results establish nonlinear X-ray diffraction as a channel-selective probe of radiation-induced dynamics and demonstrate that radiation damage can couple differently to nonlinear and linear X-ray responses.

infographic.key_insight: Nonlinear X-ray parametric down-conversion selectively probes radiation-induced dynamics in MAPbBr3, revealing behavior distinct from conventional Bragg diffraction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Comparing nonlinear and linear X-ray responses could help distinguish radiation-driven changes in hybrid perovskites that conventional diffraction alone may not resolve.
method: Measure X-ray-to-ultraviolet parametric down-conversion during continuous irradiation of a MAPbBr3 single crystal.
Compare minute-timescale PDC and Bragg diffraction dynamics.
Use density functional theory to assess electronic contributions and bromide-vacancy effects.
infographic.evidence_signal: Both signals show slow decay consistent with diffusion-driven damage, but reach different steady states; only Bragg diffraction shows an additional fast decay, while calculations implicate methylammonium N 2s states in PDC.
infographic.watch_item: The intrinsically weak PDC signal requires high photon flux, making measurement-induced damage an important constraint.
infographic.paper_title: X-ray parametric down-conversion probes radiation-induced dynamics in hybrid perovskite MAPbBr3

title: Hydrogen Thermodiffusion in Tungsten: Trapped Hydrogen Distorts Heat of Transport Estimation from Total Concentration Profiles
authors: Ville Jantunen, Daniel R. Mason, Sanjeet Kaur
abstract: We investigate hydrogen diffusion in tungsten under thermal gradients in the presence of trapping sites using multiscale simulations. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we find that the heat of transport, which quantifies the coupling between temperature gradients and hydrogen transport, for hydrogen in tungsten is positive (thermophobic) at lower temperatures but changes sign near $1000$ K. We investigate the origin of the heat of transport and find that harmonic transition state theory with elastic thermal-expansion corrections is insufficient to explain the observed behaviour, consistent with either a breakdown of local thermodynamic equilibrium or non-negligible anharmonic contributions. We further extend previous studies of hydrogen thermodiffusion by including the effect of trapping sites in both simulations and analytical models. We show that when trapped hydrogen accounts for a significant fraction of the total hydrogen concentration, the heat of transport inferred from measurements of the total concentration is dominated by the temperature dependence of the trapped hydrogen population and no longer reflects the gradient in the mobile hydrogen concentration. Consequently, experimentally measured heats of transport cannot in general be used directly in continuum-scale models that explicitly account for trapping and detrapping. In such models, the heat of transport should be based on mobile hydrogen concentrations only to avoid incorporating trapping effects twice.

infographic.key_insight: Trapped hydrogen can dominate the heat of transport inferred from total concentration profiles, masking the thermodiffusion behavior of mobile hydrogen in tungsten.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Continuum models with explicit trapping and detrapping should use a mobile-hydrogen-based heat of transport to avoid double-counting trapping effects.
method: Molecular dynamics simulations of hydrogen transport under thermal gradients.
Simulations and analytical models incorporating hydrogen trapping sites.
Comparison with harmonic transition state theory including elastic thermal-expansion corrections.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations show positive, thermophobic heat of transport at lower temperatures, a sign change near 1000 K, and trapping-driven distortion of estimates from total hydrogen concentrations.
infographic.watch_item: Harmonic transition state theory does not explain the observed behavior; local-equilibrium breakdown or anharmonic contributions remain possible explanations.
infographic.paper_title: Hydrogen Thermodiffusion in Tungsten: Trapped Hydrogen Distorts Heat of Transport Estimation from Total Concentration Profiles

title: Discovery of Kondo-Kramers Nodal Line Topological State in strongly correlated material CeAuAl$_3$
authors: Hari Bhandari, Kevin Allen, Kuan-Sen Li, Yuan Fang, Arushi, Karthik Rao
abstract: Kramers nodal lines (KNLs) are predicted in all achiral, non-centrosymmetric crystal structures, and yet there are very few experimental realizations of KNLs, only in weakly correlated systems. Especially, their realization in strongly correlated systems remains unexplored. Here we investigate KNL topology in the non-centrosymmetric, achiral Kondo lattice CeAuAl$_3$, using magnetotransport, thermodynamic measurements, density functional theory (DFT), and tight-binding toy model calculations. We find that CeAuAl$_3$ hosts KNLs in the $\mathitΓ\text{-}Z$ and $X\text{-}P$ directions, protected by time-reversal and mirror symmetries. Breaking of these crystalline symmetries, along with time-reversal symmetry via spin polarization, lifts the KNL degeneracy, which, in turn, generates Berry curvature resulting in an intrinsic anomalous Hall effect (AHE). More importantly, CeAuAl$_3$ shows large AHE not only below the magnetic ordering temperature $T_N$ but rather below the Kondo temperature. This underscores the role of the Kondo correlations in bringing the KNLs at the Fermi surface rather than at accidental energies, as would be expected without correlations. Our work identifies a new topological state, Kondo-Kramers Nodal Line, with CeAuAl$_3$ being the first compound explicitly identified to host this new correlated topological state, and demonstrating the expected AHE associated with it. More generally, our work outlines the pathway for finding Kondo-KNL systems in all compounds that combine achiral, non-centrosymmetric structure with Kondo correlations.

infographic.key_insight: CeAuAl₃ is identified as a Kondo–Kramers nodal-line material, linking strong electronic correlations with symmetry-protected topological band degeneracies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The findings offer a materials-screening strategy for correlated topological conductors that combine achiral, non-centrosymmetric crystal structures with Kondo physics.
method: Magnetotransport and thermodynamic measurements
Density functional theory calculations
Tight-binding toy models of symmetry breaking
infographic.evidence_signal: Calculations identify nodal lines along Γ–Z and X–P, while measurements show a large anomalous Hall effect below the Kondo temperature, extending above magnetic ordering.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract supports the nodal-line interpretation through calculations and transport but does not report direct spectroscopic observation.
infographic.paper_title: Discovery of Kondo-Kramers Nodal Line Topological State in strongly correlated material CeAuAl$_3$

title: Quantum benchmarks for magnetic energies and transition temperatures
authors: Mojtaba Alaei, Ilia Mikhailov, Alireza Qaiumzadeh, Artem Oganov
abstract: Predicting magnetic ordering temperatures requires accurate exchange interactions and an appropriate treatment of spin thermodynamics. Here we assess these requirements through complementary quantum Monte Carlo benchmarks. For five insulating antiferromagnets, we compare ferromagnetic-antiferromagnetic energy differences from diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) and density functional theory with references reconstructed from inelastic neutron scattering (INS) exchanges. DMC underestimates these references but achieves a mean absolute error comparable to the best-performing functionals tested. Separately, we directly test the previously proposed (S+1)/S rescaling of classical Monte Carlo temperatures against quantum stochastic series expansion simulations for 17 compounds using corresponding INS-derived Heisenberg Hamiltonians. Rescaling reduces the mean absolute classical-quantum temperature difference from 81.7 to 8.2 K, with a mean absolute percentage difference of 5.9 %. These results establish a direct quantum benchmark for the rescaling within the tested models and emphasize that improvements in electronic magnetic energy scales should be accompanied by attention to quantum spin thermodynamics.

infographic.key_insight: Rescaling classical magnetic transition temperatures by (S+1)/S closely reproduces quantum benchmarks across 17 tested compounds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable magnetic transition-temperature predictions require both accurate exchange energies and quantum-aware spin thermodynamics.
method: Benchmark DMC and DFT magnetic energy differences for five insulating antiferromagnets against INS-derived references.
Compare classical Monte Carlo temperatures with quantum stochastic series expansion results for 17 INS-derived Heisenberg models.
Test the proposed (S+1)/S temperature rescaling.
infographic.evidence_signal: Rescaling reduced the mean absolute classical–quantum temperature difference from 81.7 to 8.2 K, with a mean absolute percentage difference of 5.9%; DMC energy errors were comparable to those of the best tested functionals.
infographic.watch_item: The rescaling is validated within the tested Heisenberg models, not established as universal; DMC also systematically underestimated the energy references.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum benchmarks for magnetic energies and transition temperatures

title: Dopant Cluster Engineering for Tunable Room-Temperature Ferromagnetism in 2D Transition Metal Dichalcogenides
authors: Shivangee, Sachin Grewal, Akash Singh
abstract: Two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (2D-TMDs) offer a promising platform for realizing dilute magnetic semiconductors. However, simultaneously achieving large magnetic anisotropy energy (MAE) and high Curie temperature (T$_\text{c}$) remains a major challenge. In this work, we employ DFT+U to systematically investigate the thermodynamic stability and magnetic properties of 2D-MoSe$_2$ and 2D-WSe$_2$ doped with transition metal atoms. We found that the paired dopant configurations are more stable than previously attributed isolated dopants. Despite their nearly identical crystal structures, 2D-MoSe$_2$ and 2D-WSe$_2$ show contrasting properties upon doping. All paired dopants in 2D-MoSe$_2$ exhibit long-range ferromagnetic coupling (FMC) primarily due to carrier-mediated exchange interactions, whereas those in 2D-WSe$_2$ show weak exchange coupling. Interestingly, 2Mn$_\text{2W}$ shows a transition from less stable antiferromagnetic coupling (AFMC) in the short range to highly stable FMC in the long-range. The combined effect of spin-orbit coupling, exchange interactions, and orbital hybridization gives rise to a large MAE with maximum in-plane values of $-$3.5 meV for 2V$_\text{2Mo}$ and $-$3.2 meV for 2Mn$_\text{2W}$. Monte Carlo simulations estimate T$_\text{c}$ $\simeq$ 440 K for 2Fe$_\text{2Mo}$ and ensure its high-temperature stability in 2D-MoSe$_2$. Our results establish dopant clustering as an effective route to engineer high-temperature ferromagnetism in 2D-TMDs and highlight their potential for nano-spintronic applications.

infographic.key_insight: Paired transition-metal dopants are more stable than isolated dopants and offer a route to tunable, high-temperature ferromagnetism in 2D MoSe₂ and WSe₂.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Dopant-cluster engineering could enable atomically thin magnetic semiconductors for room-temperature nano-spintronic devices.
method: DFT+U calculations of dopant stability and magnetic properties.
Analysis of exchange coupling, spin–orbit coupling, and orbital hybridization.
Monte Carlo estimation of Curie temperature.
infographic.evidence_signal: Calculations predict long-range ferromagnetic coupling for all studied paired dopants in MoSe₂, in-plane MAE values of −3.5 meV for paired V in MoSe₂ and −3.2 meV for paired Mn in WSe₂, and a Curie temperature near 440 K for paired Fe in MoSe₂.
infographic.watch_item: These computational predictions require experimental validation, particularly controlled dopant-pair formation and magnetic stability in fabricated monolayers.
infographic.paper_title: Dopant Cluster Engineering for Tunable Room-Temperature Ferromagnetism in 2D Transition Metal Dichalcogenides
